title: Gukesh holds Sindarov to a draw as youngest World Chess Championship in history opens in Geneva
summary: Defending champion D. Gukesh survived a clock scare to draw Game 1 against Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva, opening the youngest World Chess Championship match ever played — both players are 20 — in a 14-game contest for the $2.5 million prize fund.
content:
The youngest World Chess Championship match in history began with a hard-fought draw on Tuesday, as defending champion D. Gukesh of India held challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan in the opening game in Geneva.

Both players are 20 years old, making this the first World Championship match ever contested between two players born in the 21st century. Sindarov, playing White, pressed for much of the game at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, on the outskirts of Geneva, but Gukesh defended with precision and the game ended in a draw by threefold repetition after 38 moves, according to ChessBase.

The opening was a surprise in itself. After Sindarov began with 1.e4, Gukesh steered the game into the Berlin Defence, an opening he rarely plays at this level. Sindarov came armed with deep preparation, blitzing out his early moves and introducing a novelty with 13.Ne4 that left Gukesh thinking for more than 15 minutes. By the early middlegame the challenger had built a lead of around 25 minutes on the clock, and after 21.g4 the advantage on time stretched to roughly half an hour.

Gukesh, however, refused to crack. Despite slipping into serious time trouble ahead of the move-40 time control, he found accurate defences in a queenless endgame and neutralised White's initiative, according to the Indian Express. There was a curious incident late in the game when Sindarov incorrectly claimed a draw and was penalised two minutes by the arbiters, though by then the result was effectively settled. With the score level at 0.5-0.5, Gukesh will have the White pieces in Game 2 on Wednesday.

The result leaves the match exactly where it started, but the balance of the contest is anything but even. On paper, the challenger arrives as the favourite. Sindarov is ranked world No. 4 with a rating of 2782, while Gukesh has slipped to world No. 26 since winning the title, a fall that reflects what Sportstar described as a terrible year for the champion. Sindarov is also in the form of his life: he won the 2025 FIDE World Cup in Goa, beating China's Wei Yi in the final, and then won the 2026 Candidates Tournament in Cyprus without losing a game, scoring 10 points from 14 games and clinching first place with a round to spare.

Gukesh's own road to the crown was scarcely less remarkable. He won the 2024 Candidates at 17, then defeated China's Ding Liren 7.5-6.5 in Singapore in December 2024, winning the decisive 14th game to become the youngest undisputed world champion in history at 18, breaking a record held by Garry Kasparov since 1985. He became a grandmaster at 12 and won individual gold medals at the Chess Olympiads of 2022 and 2024. Sindarov, who also became a grandmaster at 12, would become the first world champion from Uzbekistan if he wins in Geneva, and the first Uzbek ever to contest a classical title match.

The match is played over a maximum of 14 classical games, with the first player to reach 7.5 points crowned champion. Games begin at 3pm local time, with a rest day after every three games. The final scheduled classical game is on December 11, with tiebreaks, if needed, on December 12. The total prize fund is $2.5 million. Sindarov will celebrate his 21st birthday on December 8, the day Game 12 is scheduled.

The setting is unusual for a world title match. The games are being played at the Fondation Martin Bodmer, a museum and library of rare books and manuscripts, after FIDE chose a neutral venue rather than staging the match in India or Uzbekistan. The opening ceremony was held on November 22 at the Palais des Nations, home of the United Nations Office at Geneva. Geneva is often called the global capital of peace; for the next three weeks it will host a very different kind of contest.

What happens next will depend on whether Gukesh can steady himself with White in Game 2. A world championship is a different test from any tournament: it rewards preparation, nerve and stamina over three weeks rather than a single good day. Sindarov has the rating, the form and the momentum. Gukesh has the title, the experience of having won a match from behind, and the knowledge that he has already made history once. The draw in Game 1 settled nothing, and that is precisely what makes the next thirteen games worth watching.
